article_title: Programming Language Policy as an AI Literacy Equity Problem: A 15-Nation Comparative Analysis
citation: Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Iulia-Maria Popescu. (2026). Programming Language Policy as an AI Literacy Equity Problem: A 15-Nation Comparative Analysis. ALIT4ALL 2026, co-located with AIED 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0005-3547-5772
title: Japan's decoupled reform: universal Python instruction with DNCL pseudocode examination
description: Japan's 2022 Information I reform standardizes "Python for classroom instruction across all secondary schools" while a domain-specific pseudocode (DNCL) is used for the national university entrance examination. This decoupling ensures no student is disadvantaged by their Python implementation or IDE choice in high-stakes assessment, and by using pseudocode for assessment Japan "preserves the pedagogical benefits of Python while neutralizing the assessment lock-in problem" common to washback-driven systems.
requirements: A domain-specific assessment pseudocode (DNCL) maintained by the national entrance examination body
constraints: Addresses the washback tension of Model B systems by decoupling assessment language from instructional language
target_learning_goals: Universal Python-based AI literacy instruction with exam-neutral assessment
examples: The 2022 Information I curriculum uses Python for instruction; the 2025 university entrance examination uses DNCL pseudocode.
key_sources: Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Iulia-Maria Popescu. (2026). Programming Language Policy as an AI Literacy Equity Problem: A 15-Nation Comparative Analysis. ALIT4ALL 2026, co-located with AIED 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0005-3547-5772

article_title: The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions
citation: Robin Samuelsson. (2023). The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00210-w
title: Janus-faced learning: a unified account combining social transmission and individual construction
description: The article proposes a conciliatory theoretical framework named after the metaphor of a Janus face, which 'considers how learning centrally involves taking what is known and using this for future actions as the double-faced view for understanding human learning'. It argues that the dichotomy between individually constructed (Piagetian constructivist) and socially transmitted (Vygotskian sociocultural) learning is unnecessary, and that learning is 'a process pendulating between exploration and exploitation, between individual and social learning mechanisms'. Learners may rely on instructed material at one stage while constructing their own conceptions at other stages.
requirements: A complete account of learning must contain both individual-construction and social-transmission dimensions, so theories and environments must incorporate both modes
constraints: The article is a theoretical perspective, not an empirical test of the framework
target_learners: children in early childhood and primary education
target_learning_goals: understanding human learning as both individual and social; balanced educational design
examples: Guided play scenarios, Montessori schools, and Tools-of-the-Mind programmes are described as pedagogical alternatives that incorporate both poles in balanced learning environments
key_sources: Robin Samuelsson. (2023). The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00210-w

article_title: From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework
citation: Garry Falloon. (2020). From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09767-4
title: Janssen et al.'s twelve-element digital competence model organises core, supportive and dispositional competencies as building blocks
description: Janssen et al.'s (2013) Delphi study of 95 experts from academic, education, government/policy and IT business sectors identified twelve elements essential to broadly-based digital competence, summarised in the article's Table 1 (e.g., functional, integrative, specialised, communication and collaboration, information management, privacy and security, legal and ethical, technology and society, learning with and about technology, informed decision making, coherence/self-efficacy, dispositional). The article reports they conceptualised each element as a 'building block', with core competencies enhanced by networking and information management capabilities and parallel supportive competencies covering legal/ethical, societal-impact and dispositional factors. The TDC framework builds directly on this model by positioning its general competencies within teacher education.
requirements: Digital competence should be understood as a pluralistic concept, viewed from a plurality of angles, with balance struck between over-inclusive and too-restrictive common denominators
constraints: The authors signal limitations to direct application to specific contexts: development and display of digital competence differs across contexts
target_learners: teacher educators designing digital capability programmes
target_learning_goals: holistic digital competence spanning technical, ethical, societal and dispositional elements
examples: The article's Table 1 explains each of the twelve competency areas with the knowledge and understanding it covers
key_sources: Garry Falloon. (2020). From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09767-4

citation: Patricia A. Young. (2021). Creation in shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09958-7
title: Jastudy: a CALL program for Japanese functional expressions for Chinese-speaking learners
description: Jastudy is a Computer-Assisted Language Learning program developed by Liu et al. (2019) that "helps Chinese speaking second language learners master Japanese functional expressions." The editorial describes building such a system as a task requiring mastery of language, literacy and computer science expertise, and presents Jastudy as an example of creating technologies to meet community language and literacy needs within the shifting-to-digital revolution.
requirements: The editorial states that constructing a CALL system requires a mastery of language, literacy and computer science expertise.
target_learners: Chinese-speaking second language learners of Japanese
examples: Liu et al. (2019) developed Jastudy to address the difficulty Chinese-speaking learners have with Japanese functional expressions.
key_sources: Patricia A. Young. (2021). Creation in shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09958-7

article_title: Meta-Analysis of Jelajah Alam Sekitar (JAS) Approach Implementation in Learning Process
citation: S. Ngabekti, S. Ridlo, E. Peniati, R. Martanto. (2017). META-ANALYSIS OF JELAJAH ALAM SEKITAR (JAS) APPROACH IMPLEMENTATION IN LEARNING PROCESS. Jurnal Pendidikan IPA Indonesia. https://doi.org/10.15294/jpii.v6i1.8490
title: Jelajah Alam Sekitar (JAS) approach with six defining characteristics
description: JAS is a learning approach that "uses the student's nature environment, whether the physical, social, technology, or culture environment as the learning object in biology" whose phenomena are learned through scientific work. It is characterized by six components — exploration, constructivism, science process, learning community, edutainment, and authentic assessment — integrated into indoor and outdoor learning. Developed by the Biology Department of FMIPA UNNES since 2005, it spread to eight Indonesian provinces and has been studied from primary school to college.
requirements: The six components (exploration, science process, constructivism, learning community, and authentic assessment) should be integrated into both indoor and outdoor learning for JAS to be well implemented
constraints: Users noted JAS needs clearer criteria distinguishing it from CTL so it is not just another name for contextual learning
target_learners: primary school to university students in Indonesia
examples: Implemented with role playing in an Islamic boarding school ecosystem subject, in Biostatistics, and in Animal Ecology, using environments such as grass fields, the UNNES educational tour garden, and soy sauce fermentation observation
key_sources: S. Ngabekti, S. Ridlo, E. Peniati, R. Martanto. (2017). META-ANALYSIS OF JELAJAH ALAM SEKITAR (JAS) APPROACH IMPLEMENTATION IN LEARNING PROCESS. Jurnal Pendidikan IPA Indonesia. https://doi.org/10.15294/jpii.v6i1.8490

article_title: Meta-Analysis of Jelajah Alam Sekitar (JAS) Approach Implementation in Learning Process
citation: S. Ngabekti, S. Ridlo, E. Peniati, R. Martanto. (2017). META-ANALYSIS OF JELAJAH ALAM SEKITAR (JAS) APPROACH IMPLEMENTATION IN LEARNING PROCESS. Jurnal Pendidikan IPA Indonesia. https://doi.org/10.15294/jpii.v6i1.8490
title: JAS approach development and tracer study at UNNES Biology Department
description: The Biology Department of FMIPA UNNES has developed the Jelajah Alam Sekitar learning approach since 2005. A tracer study by Ridlo (2005) and Ridlo et al. (2016) shows that "since 2006 to 2016, JAS has been spread in eight provinces in Indonesia although most of it are in Central Java especially in Semarang", and that JAS has been researched from elementary school to university, tracked mostly with quantitative pre- and quasi-experiment designs.
requirements: Departmental commitment to analyzing JAS characteristics and publishing research results
constraints: Information about JAS is still rare in printed and electronic media, per the user survey
target_learners: Indonesian students from primary school to college
target_learning_goals: biology learning through direct experience of the natural environment
examples: Tracer studies documentary and online; 106 research titles analyzed in the meta-analysis from UNNES, UPGRIS, and internet library sources
key_sources: S. Ngabekti, S. Ridlo, E. Peniati, R. Martanto. (2017). META-ANALYSIS OF JELAJAH ALAM SEKITAR (JAS) APPROACH IMPLEMENTATION IN LEARNING PROCESS. Jurnal Pendidikan IPA Indonesia. https://doi.org/10.15294/jpii.v6i1.8490

article_title: "Diagnose, Treat, and SUPPORT". Clinical competencies in the management of older adults with aspiration pneumonia: a scoping review.
citation: Yoshimatsu Yuki, Ohtake Yoichi, Ukai Mamiko, Miyagami Taiju, Morikawa Toru, Shimamura Yoshinosuke, Kataoka Yuki, Hashimoto Tadayuki. (2023). “Diagnose, Treat, and SUPPORT”. Clinical competencies in the management of older adults with aspiration pneumonia: a scoping review. European Geriatric Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41999-023-00898-4
title: JAPEP preliminary competency framework developed by simplified Delphi method
description: A preliminary list of nine clinical competencies (diagnosis, treatment, swallow assessment, medication management, nutrition assessment, oral care, rehabilitation, multidisciplinary team, and ethics) developed by members of the Japan Aspiration pneumonia inter-Professional team Educational Program (JAPEP) — six general practitioners, a rehabilitation physician, respiratory physician, psychosomatic physician, dentist and pharmacologist. The article states the members developed the list "using a simplified Delphi method", chosen because it "has been considered superior to more informal methods of expert opinion". This list was then refined by the scoping review into the 12-competency framework.
requirements: Multidisciplinary expert membership with clinical and academic experience in aspiration pneumonia management
constraints: Developed as a simplified rather than full Delphi process, a limitation the authors acknowledge
target_learners: Multidisciplinary healthcare professionals in acute healthcare settings managing older adults with aspiration pneumonia
target_learning_goals: Defining the clinical competencies needed to manage aspiration pneumonia in older adults
examples: JAPEP members produced the initial nine-competency list that the scoping review subsequently expanded and renamed
key_sources: Yoshimatsu Yuki, Ohtake Yoichi, Ukai Mamiko, Miyagami Taiju, Morikawa Toru, Shimamura Yoshinosuke, Kataoka Yuki, Hashimoto Tadayuki. (2023). “Diagnose, Treat, and SUPPORT”. Clinical competencies in the management of older adults with aspiration pneumonia: a scoping review. European Geriatric Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41999-023-00898-4

article_title: Languaging and Writing Skill: The Effect of Collaborative Writing on EFL Students' Writing Performance
citation: Mohammad Khatib, Hussein Meihami. (2015). Languaging and Writing Skill: The Effect of Collaborative Writing on EFL Students' Writing Performance. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.1p.203
title: Jacobs et al. (1981) paragraph rating scale for assessing five writing components
description: The study's assessment instrument is the paragraph rating scale first proposed by Jacobs, Zinkgraf, Wormuth, Hartfiel, and Hughey (1981) and modified by Hedgcock and Lefkowitz (1991). It "defines the following five component areas on s 0-100 point scale": content, organization, grammar, vocabulary, and mechanics of writing, with four bands per component (excellent to very good, good to average, fair to poor, very poor). Two trained assessors used it to score pretest and posttest paragraphs.
requirements: Two assessors trained on the scale to establish inter-rater reliability
constraints: Applied to at-least-100-word paragraphs written in 30 minutes in this study
target_learning_goals: assessing overall writing performance and its five components
examples: Used to score 'Describe your dream home' pretest and 'Where do you like to travel? Why?' posttest paragraphs
key_sources: Mohammad Khatib, Hussein Meihami. (2015). Languaging and Writing Skill: The Effect of Collaborative Writing on EFL Students' Writing Performance. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.1p.203

article_title: Impact of Attached File Formats on the Performance of ChatGPT-4 on the Japanese National Nursing Examination: Evaluation Study.
citation: Taira K, Itaya T, Yada S, Hiyama K, Hanada A. (2025). Impact of Attached File Formats on the Performance of ChatGPT-4 on the Japanese National Nursing Examination: Evaluation Study. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/67197
title: Japanese National Nursing Examination evaluation dataset in five prompt file formats
description: An evaluation dataset built from the publicly released 2023 Japanese National Nursing Examination: "all 50 basic knowledge questions" plus 190 general questions, prepared in TEXT (.txt), DOCX (.docx), PDF (.pdf), IMAGE (.jpg), and a PROMPT-ONLY format that described all questions directly in the prompt. The passing standard for the basic knowledge questions was approximately 80%. CSV, JSON, XML, and Markdown were excluded to maintain consistency and focus on common formats.
requirements: Files were made viewable via OpenAI's API ASSISTANT (type = retrieval) function, with prompts per format summarized in Textbox 1
constraints: The article excluded CSV, JSON, XML, and Markdown formats "to maintain consistency and focus on more common formats"
target_learners: nursing education researchers evaluating generative AI
target_learning_goals: assessing large language model performance on nursing licensing examination content
key_sources: Taira K, Itaya T, Yada S, Hiyama K, Hanada A. (2025). Impact of Attached File Formats on the Performance of ChatGPT-4 on the Japanese National Nursing Examination: Evaluation Study. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/67197

article_title: UK and Ireland Joint Advisory Group (JAG) consensus statements for training and certification in diagnostic endoscopic ultrasound (EUS).
citation: El Menabawey Tareq, McCrudden Raymond, Shetty Dushyant, Hopper Andrew D, Huggett Matthew T, Bekkali Noor, Carroll Nicholas R, Henry Elaine, Johnson Gavin J, Keane Margaret G, Love Mark, McKay Colin J, Norton Sally, Oppong Kofi, Penman Ian, Ramesh Jayapal, Ryan Barbara, Siau Keith, Nayar Manu. (2024). UK and Ireland Joint Advisory Group (JAG) consensus statements for training and certification in diagnostic endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). Gut. https://doi.org/10.1136/gutjnl-2023-329800
title: JAG four-domain framework for EUS training and certification with a three-stage case-volume syllabus
description: A competency-based certification framework for diagnostic EUS organised into four domains: definition of competence (13 statements), acquisition of competence (10), assessment of competence (5) and postcertification mentorship (5), developed via a modified Delphi process with GRADE appraisal and 80% agreement thresholds. The panel proposes "a syllabus divided into three domains: (1) ‘early novice’ (0–75 cases), (2) ‘intermediate’ (76–150 cases) and (3) ‘advanced’ (151–250 cases)" with categories spanning background knowledge, scope handling, console use, anatomy, image interpretation and tissue acquisition, culminating in the complete EUS procedure.
requirements: Requires a JETS e-portfolio logbook of procedures, formative DOPS assessments, and attendance at a JAG-accredited basic EUS skills course
constraints: Scope excludes therapeutic EUS, rectal EUS and endobronchial ultrasound, paediatric EUS, upskilling established endoscopists, and trainees trained mostly outside the UK
target_learners: advanced endoscopy trainees in the UK and Ireland
target_learning_goals: independent diagnostic EUS practice including image acquisition, interpretation, tissue acquisition and non-technical skills
examples: The pathway was launched alongside the JETS EUS logbook, and the panel states "Data from JETS will provide a national picture on trainees’ progress, which will inform future research on learning curves on EUS."
key_sources: El Menabawey Tareq, McCrudden Raymond, Shetty Dushyant, Hopper Andrew D, Huggett Matthew T, Bekkali Noor, Carroll Nicholas R, Henry Elaine, Johnson Gavin J, Keane Margaret G, Love Mark, McKay Colin J, Norton Sally, Oppong Kofi, Penman Ian, Ramesh Jayapal, Ryan Barbara, Siau Keith, Nayar Manu. (2024). UK and Ireland Joint Advisory Group (JAG) consensus statements for training and certification in diagnostic endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). Gut. https://doi.org/10.1136/gutjnl-2023-329800

article_title: Virtual versus jaw simulation in inlay preparation preclinical teaching: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Sheng Jie, Zhang Congdi, Gao Zhengkun, Yan Yimin, Meng Yucheng, Ren Shiqi, Liu Bin, Zhang Baoping. (2022). Virtual versus jaw simulation in inlay preparation preclinical teaching: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03930-6
title: Jaw simulation model (Type II, NISSIN) for preclinical dental skills training
description: The conventional jaw model (Type II, NISSIN, Japan) used for medical experimental teaching and preclinical skills training, on which stomatology undergraduates practise adjusting chair position, applying examination instruments, selecting fulcrums, and performing dental preparation and restoration. Training on the jaw model "allows the subjects to become more familiar with the clinical operation". The article concludes the traditional jaw model could not be eliminated or replaced in inlay preparation training.
requirements: Physical simulation providing actual clinical tactile feeling and timely correction of errors in depth and extent of tooth preparation
constraints: This method is more time-consuming and expensive with few models, and cannot simulate the common and difficult cases in the clinical practice of real situations
target_learning_goals: Inlay tooth preparation on extracted teeth
examples: Groups J received 2 hours of jaw model training, while combined groups received 1 hour on the jaw model paired with 1 hour on the virtual system
key_sources: Sheng Jie, Zhang Congdi, Gao Zhengkun, Yan Yimin, Meng Yucheng, Ren Shiqi, Liu Bin, Zhang Baoping. (2022). Virtual versus jaw simulation in inlay preparation preclinical teaching: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03930-6

article_title: Medical students as adverse drug event managers, learning about side effects while improving their reporting in clinical practice.
citation: Reumerman M., Tichelaar J., Richir M.C., van Agtmael M.A. (2021). Medical students as adverse drug event managers, learning about side effects while improving their reporting in clinical practice. Naunyn-Schmiedeberg's Archives of Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00210-021-02060-y
title: Junior-Adverse Drug Event Manager (J-ADEM) team: a student-run four-step ADR detection, diagnosis, and reporting program
description: The J-ADEM team is a weekly team of two volunteer medical students (1st–6th year) embedded in the Learner-Centered Student-Run Clinic, tasked to "systematically screen patients hospitalized for a suspected serious or unknown ADR." Its procedure "consisted of four consecutive steps": identifying patients with potential ADRs by screening or consultation, reviewing the electronic patient record and performing a medication and side effect interview, applying the four BAT-M diagnostic criteria, reporting the ADR to the Netherlands Pharmacovigilance Center Lareb, and feeding Lareb's feedback back to the attending physician and the patient record.
requirements: Students participate voluntarily within a learner-centered student-run clinic and are supervised by a clinical pharmacologist who reviews each suspected ADR with the student and the attending physician
constraints: Evaluated on only two of 23 wards (internal medicine and ENT) in a single tertiary academic hospital; patients with deliberate or unintentional overdose were excluded
target_learners: medical students in the bachelor phase (1st–6th year)
target_learning_goals: clinical pharmacovigilance skills: ADR detection, diagnosis, and reporting
examples: Over one year, the team screened 136 patients, submitted 65 ADR reports to Lareb (50 classified as severe, 77%), and performed on average 5.2 consultations per participating student (range 1–9)
key_sources: Reumerman M., Tichelaar J., Richir M.C., van Agtmael M.A. (2021). Medical students as adverse drug event managers, learning about side effects while improving their reporting in clinical practice. Naunyn-Schmiedeberg's Archives of Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00210-021-02060-y

article_title: Impact of a national basic skills in colonoscopy course on trainee performance: An interrupted time series analysis.
citation: Siau K, Hodson J, Anderson JT, Valori R, Smith G, Hagan P, Iacucci M, Dunckley P. (2020). Impact of a national basic skills in colonoscopy course on trainee performance: An interrupted time series analysis. World Journal of Gastroenterology. https://doi.org/10.3748/wjg.v26.i23.3283
title: Basic skills in colonoscopy (BSC) course: a three-day JAG-accredited hands-on training course mandatory for UK provisional colonoscopy certification
description: The BSC is a national UK training course introduced to standardise colonoscopy training and mandatory for provisional certification since 2011. The article describes it as "an intensive, three-day course consisting of hands-on, supervised patient-based colonoscopy", complemented by mechanical simulator training, teaching of basic principles, small-group discussions and performance-enhancing feedback. Trainees undertake 4-6 patient-based cases under expert faculty supervision, with tri-split video streams mediating group reflection and one-to-one teaching built around individualised learning objectives.
requirements: Trainees require written support from their educational supervisor or endoscopy trainer to attend
trainees must have at least one training list per week available at their base hospital following the course
constraints: Courses must be delivered in JAG accredited training centres by accredited faculty who had attended endoscopy-related Train-the-Trainer courses
target_learners: UK colonoscopy trainees (gastroenterology, colorectal surgery, non-medical endoscopists, general practitioners)
target_learning_goals: Basic skills and competencies for performing colonoscopy independently, including technical and non-technical skills
examples: The study analysed 369 trainees who attended 202 BSC courses between 2011 and 2016
key_sources: Siau K, Hodson J, Anderson JT, Valori R, Smith G, Hagan P, Iacucci M, Dunckley P. (2020). Impact of a national basic skills in colonoscopy course on trainee performance: An interrupted time series analysis. World Journal of Gastroenterology. https://doi.org/10.3748/wjg.v26.i23.3283
